Alert System: scoring the functional consequences of an in-silico perturbation

alertsystem_tutorial.Rmd

compact can impose module-level changes onto control cells in silico (ModulePerturbation), but a perturbed expression matrix on its own does not tell you what the cell is now doing differently. The Alert System is the scoring layer that answers that question: it takes a baseline assay and a virtually perturbed assay from the same cells, and reports, pathway by pathway, how strongly and how consistently essential cellular programs respond.

Because every cell contributes a paired measurement (its own pre and its own post), the Alert System is not a differential-expression test between two groups of cells. It is a within-cell contrast, which removes the cell-to-cell variation that usually dominates single-cell pathway scoring and lets us ask a question that bulk-style summaries cannot: does the pathway respond in a few cells very strongly, or in most cells a little?

The question this tutorial is built around

Single-cell and single-nucleus profiling characterize only the cells recovered and retained after sample preparation, sequencing, and quality control. When a perturbation is lethal or severely destabilizing, the most affected cells are selectively lost, and what remains is a population that either compensated or was resilient to begin with. Conventional summaries — cell-type proportions, differential expression — can look unremarkable precisely because the informative cells are gone.

We work through exactly that situation. For this tutorial we use the in vivo AAV-Perturb-seq dataset from Santinha et al. 2023, which applied pooled CRISPR–Cas9 screening with snRNA-seq to the adult mouse prefrontal cortex, targeting mouse homologues of genes in the 22q11.2 locus. The original study identified substantial transcriptional responses to all perturbations, but excluded Ufd1l from downstream validation because its response was enriched for a broad disruption of proteostasis rather than a clean gene-specific phenotype.

Ufd1l is a paradox worth chasing. The goal of the gene silencing was to eliminate target expression, yet conventional differential expression reports Ufd1l as significantly upregulated in the CRISPR-treated population — and, as we will see below, most Ufd1l-targeted nuclei score near the Safe_H control on a perturbation-strength scale. A misleading transcript-level increase coupled with an apparent absence of perturbed cell states points to survivor bias: nuclei carrying the strongest disruptions were selectively depleted, leaving behind a compensating or resilient remainder.

So the analysis proceeds in four steps, and the tutorial follows them in order:

  1. Look at the data. Confirm the cell types and check whether the perturbation produces any gross population shift on the UMAP.
  2. Quantify perturbation strength with Mixscale. Establish that Ufd1l-targeted nuclei do not separate from control, which is the observation that motivates everything after it.
  3. Impose the module change in silico with compact. Take the module alterations observed in the surviving perturbed cells and apply them to control cells, so we can ask what those changes would do.
  4. Score the consequences with the Alert System. Find the stress-associated programs that the module change predicts — the signature that was hidden.

Setup 

# single-cell analysis package
library(Seurat)

# plotting and data science packages
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(patchwork)

# co-expression network analysis packages
library(WGCNA)
library(hdWGCNA)

# using the cowplot theme for ggplot
theme_set(theme_cowplot())

# load compact library
library(compact)

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(12345)

# optionally enable multithreading
# enableWGCNAThreads(nThreads = 8)

Set up the output directories up front, so figures and intermediate objects land in predictable places:

out_dir <- "compact_Updates/Ufd1l/"
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

data_out <- paste0(out_dir, "data/")
fig_dir  <- paste0(out_dir, "figures/")

if (!dir.exists(data_out)) dir.create(data_out, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
if (!dir.exists(fig_dir))  dir.create(fig_dir,  showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# set the working directory
setwd(data_out)
getwd()

Why setwd(). hdWGCNA writes the topological overlap matrix to a TOM/ subdirectory relative to the working directory. Setting it explicitly here keeps those files with the rest of the analysis output rather than wherever the session happened to start.

Loading the dataset

Processed data for Santinha et al. 2023 are deposited in GEO under accession GSE236519. This tutorial uses the pooled screen driven by the CBh promoter (GSE236519_pooled_screen_CBh), subset to neurons and to the Safe_H control plus the four perturbations with the strongest transcriptional phenotypes: Dgcr8, Dgcr14, Gnb1l, and Ufd1l.

The object has already been processed with hdWGCNA to construct a co-expression network (modules named CBh-M1 … CBh-M9).


# GSE236519_pooled_screen_CBh
seu_CBh_neurons <- subset(GSE236519_pooled_screen_CBh, per_gene %in% c('Safe_H', 'Dgcr8', 'Dgcr14', 'Gnb1l', 'Ufd1l'))
seu_CBh_neurons <- subset(seu_CBh_neurons, cell_types_broad %in% c('Deep_layer_neurons', 'Supp_layer_neurons', 'Interneurons'))

# hdWGCNA processed data
seu_CBh_neurons
An object of class Seurat
30556 features across 5670 samples within 1 assay
Active assay: RNA (30556 features, 2000 variable features)
 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data
 2 dimensional reductions calculated: pca, umap
table(seu_CBh_neurons$per_gene)
Dgcr14  Dgcr8  Gnb1l Safe_H  Ufd1l
   870   1666    487   2220    427

Note the group sizes: Ufd1l has the fewest recovered nuclei of any perturbation (427), despite being targeted in the same pooled screen. That is the first quiet hint of selective depletion.

Visualizing the dataset

Before any perturbation modeling, look at the data. We want to know two things: whether the cell-type annotations are clean, and whether the perturbed nuclei occupy their own region of the embedding or are intermixed with control.

First, copy the UMAP coordinates into the metadata so we can plot them with ggplot2 directly and control the aesthetics precisely:

identical(rownames(seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data),
          rownames(seu_CBh_neurons@reductions$umap@cell.embeddings))
# [1] TRUE

UMAP_df <- seu_CBh_neurons@reductions$umap@cell.embeddings
identical(rownames(seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data), rownames(UMAP_df))
# [1] TRUE

# add the UMAP coordinates to the metadata
for (meta in colnames(UMAP_df)) {
  seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data[[meta]] <-
    UMAP_df[match(rownames(seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data), rownames(UMAP_df)), meta]
}

Define consistent color schemes so the same colors carry through every figure in the project:

library(ggrastr)

color_scheme_per_gene <- list(
  "Safe_H" = "#D9D9D9",  # light gray control
  "Dgcr8"  = "#CC4C4C",  # soft modern red
  "Dgcr14" = "#4C72B0",  # scientific blue
  "Gnb1l"  = "#E2A84A",  # muted gold
  "Ufd1l"  = "#7A3178"   # plum / berry
)

color_scheme_ct <- list(
  "Deep_layer_neurons" = "#355C7D",  # muted deep blue-slate
  "Interneurons"       = "#C06C84",  # soft rosy orchid
  "Supp_layer_neurons" = "#6C5B7B"   # muted lavender-indigo
)
# UMAP_1 -> umap_1 ; UMAP_2 -> umap_2
p1 <- seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = umap_1, y = umap_2, color = cell_types_broad)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = color_scheme_ct) +
  rasterise(geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5), dpi = 600) +
  ggtitle("Cell Types") +
  umap_theme

p2 <- seu_CBh_neurons@meta.data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = umap_1, y = umap_2, color = per_gene)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = color_scheme_per_gene) +
  rasterise(geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5), dpi = 600) +
  ggtitle("Per Gene") +
  umap_theme

pdf(paste0(fig_dir, 'UMAP_seu_CBh_neurons_celltypes_n_pergene.pdf'),
    height = 6, width = 16)
p1 + p2
dev.off()

The left panel shows the three broad neuronal classes. The right panel is the one that matters for our question: the perturbed nuclei are distributed across the same regions as the Safe_H control, with no perturbation-specific cluster and no obvious shift in cell-type composition. A standard reading of this figure would be “the perturbations did not produce distinct cell states” — and that reading is exactly what we are going to challenge.

Note. rasterise() from ggrastr rasterizes only the point layer while keeping axes and text as vectors. With thousands of nuclei this keeps the PDF small and openable in Illustrator without flattening the labels.

Quantifying perturbation strength with Mixscale

A UMAP tells you about global structure, not about how strongly each individual nucleus responded. For that we use Mixscale, which assigns every cell a continuous perturbation score measuring how far its expression has moved from the non-targeting control in the direction characteristic of its assigned perturbation.

Where Mixscale comes from. Mixscale is not part of compact. It is a separate R package from the Satija lab (satijalab.github.io/Mixscale, source at github.com/longmanz/Mixscale), which extends the mixscape workflow introduced in Seurat. The two functions used below come from different places:

  • CalcPerturbSig() is a Seurat function (part of the original mixscape workflow). It computes a local perturbation signature by subtracting, from each cell, the average expression of its nearest non-targeting neighbors in PCA space. This removes confounding technical and cell-state variation before scoring.
  • RunMixscale() is from the Mixscale package. Where mixscape makes a binary perturbed / non-perturbed call, Mixscale returns a continuous score, which is what lets us see that a perturbation produced a graded response — or, as here, almost none at all.

Install it separately (remotes::install_github("longmanz/Mixscale")) and cite it alongside compact; it is doing independent work in this analysis.

library(ggridges)
library(ggplot2)
library(Mixscale)

# calculate perturbation signatures (Seurat / mixscape)
seu_CBh_neurons <- CalcPerturbSig(
  object         = seu_CBh_neurons,
  assay          = "RNA",
  slot           = "data",
  gd.class       = "per_gene",
  nt.cell.class  = "Safe_H",
  reduction      = "pca",
  ndims          = 20,
  num.neighbors  = 20,
  new.assay.name = "MixScale",
  split.by       = NULL  # metadata column if multiple biological contexts exist
)

# Mixscale: continuous perturbation scores
seu_CBh_neurons <- RunMixscale(
  object          = seu_CBh_neurons,
  assay           = "MixScale",
  slot            = "scale.data",
  labels          = "per_gene",
  nt.class.name   = "Safe_H",
  min.de.genes    = 5,
  logfc.threshold = 0.2,
  de.assay        = "RNA",
  max.de.genes    = 100,
  new.class.name  = "mixscale_score",
  fine.mode       = FALSE,
  verbose         = FALSE,
  split.by        = NULL
)

Put the control first so the ridge plot reads left to right as a comparison against baseline:

gene_order <- c("Safe_H", "Dgcr14", "Dgcr8", "Gnb1l", "Ufd1l")

seu_CBh_neurons$per_gene <- factor(
  seu_CBh_neurons$per_gene,
  levels = gene_order
)
# check the distribution of the scores for each perturbation
p <- RidgePlot(
  seu_CBh_neurons,
  features = "mixscale_score",
  group.by = "per_gene"
) + NoLegend()

pdf(paste0(fig_dir, 'RidgePlot_mixscale_score.pdf'), width = 4, height = 4)
p
dev.off()

This is the observation the rest of the tutorial exists to explain. Dgcr8, Gnb1l, and Dgcr14 targeting produces distinct populations with elevated Mixscale scores — a graded, detectable response. Most Ufd1l-targeted nuclei instead sit near the Safe_H control, with only a subset reaching higher scores.

Read together with the conventional differential expression result — Ufd1l appearing upregulated in the CRISPR-treated population, the opposite of what gene silencing should produce — the pattern suggests a complex biological phenotype rather than a simple failure of the knockout. Nuclei harboring the strongest Ufd1l disruptions were likely selectively depleted, leaving behind a population that is either compensating for the genetic insult or that was resilient from the start.

If that is true, the informative cells are not in the dataset and no amount of re-testing the surviving cells will recover them. What we can do is take the module-level changes that are still visible in the survivors, impose them on control cells in silico, and ask what those changes would do to essential cellular programs. That is the next section.

In-silico module perturbation

We apply the perturbation to the Safe_H control cells only. This is deliberate: imposing an observed module change onto healthy control cells asks “what would happen to a normal neuron if this module moved?”, which is a cleaner counterfactual than perturbing cells that are already perturbed (and already selected).

# make a copy containing only the control cells
seurat_obj <- seu_CBh_neurons %>% subset(per_gene == "Safe_H")

seurat_obj
An object of class Seurat
30556 features across 2220 samples within 1 assay
Active assay: RNA (30556 features, 2000 variable features)
 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data
 2 dimensional reductions calculated: pca, umap

Inspect the co-expression network that hdWGCNA built:

# optional, if not already present:
# add module eigengenes (MEs) to the metadata
MEs <- GetMEs(seurat_obj)
head(MEs)

modules <- GetModules(seurat_obj)
modules['Ufd1', ]
     gene_name module     color kME_CBh-M1  kME_grey  kME_CBh-M2  kME_CBh-M3
Ufd1      Ufd1 CBh-M1 turquoise 0.08039656 0.1009212 0.007428157 -0.06576732
      kME_CBh-M4  kME_CBh-M5 kME_CBh-M6 kME_CBh-M7  kME_CBh-M8 kME_CBh-M9
Ufd1 -0.01516595 -0.01295234  0.1026164 -0.0457743 -0.02771402 0.05599821

Ufd1 itself is assigned to module CBh-M1, which is one reason that module is the one we downregulate below. The directions we impose, though, come from the data rather than from module membership: differential module eigengene (DME) analysis in hdWGCNA — run upstream of this tutorial and described in the paper, so not repeated here — identified CBh-M6 as upregulated and CBh-M1 as downregulated in the surviving Ufd1l nuclei relative to the Safe_H control. In other words, we are not inventing a perturbation: we are reconstructing the module state the perturbed cells actually ended up in, and asking what that state would do to a healthy neuron.

Applying the module perturbations

ModulePerturbation() moves a module’s hub genes in the specified direction and propagates the change through the cell–cell graph, producing a new assay holding the perturbed expression matrix.

# apply the up-regulation of module CBh-M6
perturbation_name <- 'M6_up'

seurat_obj <- ModulePerturbation(
  seurat_obj,
  mod               = "CBh-M6",
  perturb_dir       = 1,
  perturbation_name = perturbation_name,
  graph             = 'RNA_nn',
  n_hubs            = 10,
  delta_scale       = 2,
  n_iters           = 10,      # default is 3
  row_normalize     = TRUE,
  use_velocyto      = FALSE,
  n_workers         = 1
)

# apply the down-regulation of module CBh-M1
perturbation_name2 <- 'M1_down'

seurat_obj <- ModulePerturbation(
  seurat_obj,
  mod               = "CBh-M1",
  perturb_dir       = -1,
  perturbation_name = perturbation_name2,
  graph             = 'RNA_nn',
  n_hubs            = 10,
  delta_scale       = 2,
  n_iters           = 10,
  row_normalize     = TRUE,
  use_velocyto      = FALSE,
  n_workers         = 1
)

seurat_obj
An object of class Seurat
91668 features across 2220 samples within 3 assays
Active assay: RNA (30556 features, 2000 variable features)
 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data
 2 other assays present: M6_up, M1_down
 2 dimensional reductions calculated: pca, umap

The two perturbations are modeled together because that is what was observed in the surviving Ufd1l nuclei: a combined module upregulation alongside the downregulation of CBh-M1 relative to the Safe_H control. Scoring them jointly (see Combining perturbations) asks what the joint state does, which is not the same question as scoring each alone.

Loading the pathway database

LoadAlertSystemPathways() returns a named list of gene vectors. It resolves gene sets from three sources, in this order:

  1. an explicit path you supply,
  2. the inst/extdata directory shipped with the installed package,
  3. an optional download from GitHub (allow_download = TRUE).
genetype <- "mouse"   # or "human"

gene_sets_mouse <- LoadAlertSystemPathways(
  genetype = "mouse",
  database = "MSigDBhallmark"
)

gene_sets <- gene_sets_mouse

length(gene_sets)
head(names(gene_sets))

Files are looked up by the pattern <database>_gene_sets_<genetype>.rds, so a local copy is found with:

alertdatabasePATH <- "AlertSystem/data/"

gene_sets_mouse <- LoadAlertSystemPathways(
  path     = alertdatabasePATH,   # optional
  genetype = "mouse",
  database = "MSigDBhallmark"
)

Where the hallmark gene sets come from

The bundled MSigDBhallmark sets are the MSigDB hallmark (H) collection, cleaned up and stored as an .rds of named character vectors. A copy of the cleaned mouse and human gene lists is archived on Zenodo alongside this project. If you want to rebuild them from the primary source, or update to a newer MSigDB release:

  • Human — the H: hallmark gene sets collection, file h.all.v<version>.Hs.symbols.gmt, from the MSigDB downloads page.
  • Mouse — the MH: hallmark gene sets collection, file mh.all.v<version>.Mm.symbols.gmt, from the mouse MSigDB collections page. These are native mouse-symbol sets, not naively ortholog-mapped human sets.
  • From R — the msigdbr package (msigdbr(species = "Mus musculus", collection = "H")) or the WEHI R-format MSigDB distributions give you the same content without a manual download.

A .gmt file converts to the expected format in two lines:

gmt <- clusterProfiler::read.gmt("mh.all.v2024.1.Mm.symbols.gmt")
gene_sets <- split(gmt$gene, gmt$term)

Custom pathways

gene_sets is just a named list, so any pathway collection works — your own curated signatures, a module gene list, a published signature table:

gene_sets_custom <- list(
  "UPR_core"        = c("Hspa5", "Ddit3", "Atf4", "Xbp1", "Eif2ak3", "Ern1"),
  "OxPhos_complexI" = c("Ndufa1", "Ndufa2", "Ndufb3", "Ndufs1", "Ndufs2"),
  "Glycolysis_core" = c("Hk2", "Pfkl", "Pkm", "Ldha", "Slc2a1")
)

Pathways are intersected with the features present in both assays, and any pathway left with fewer than min_genes detected genes is dropped. Keep an eye on the gene_coverage column in the output — a hallmark set reduced from 200 genes to 7 is still scored, but it is no longer the pathway you think it is.

Running AlertSystemScore 

AS_dir <- paste0(fig_dir, "AlertSystem/")
if (!dir.exists(AS_dir)) dir.create(AS_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# what biological replicate structure is available?
table(seurat_obj$lane)
perturbation_name <- 'M6_up'

alert_v2 <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj        = seurat_obj,
  gene_sets         = gene_sets,
  perturbation_name = "M6_up",       # the perturbed assay
  baseline_assay    = "RNA",         # the pre state

  # group.by = "cell_types_broad",
  # sample.by = "donor_id",

  score_methods = "expression",      # or c("expression", "ucell")
  summary_fun   = "trimmed_mean",

  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  ucell_response_threshold      = 0.005,

  null_unit      = "auto",
  n_permutations = 2000,

  return_details = TRUE
)

What the function does, step by step

  1. Validate. Checks assays exist, method names are legal, and flags are logical. If "ucell" is requested but the UCell package is missing, it warns and falls back to expression scoring.

  2. Align. Confirms both assays hold the same cells and features, then puts them in the same order.

  3. Filter gene sets. Keeps pathways with at least min_genes detected features, recording the original set size so coverage can be reported.

  4. Score, paired. One response per cell × pathway × method. For the expression channel, the per-cell pathway response is the mean over pathway genes of the per-gene change:

    Δp,c=1|p|∑g∈p(postg,c−preg,c)\Delta_{p,c} \;=\; \frac{1}{|p|}\sum_{g \in p} \bigl(\text{post}_{g,c} - \text{pre}_{g,c}\bigr)

    where pre and post are log-normalized values from the layer argument ("data" by default).

  5. Label direct vs. propagated genes. Using the counts layers, genes changed directly by the perturbation are distinguished from genes that changed only through network propagation. These are annotations only — they do not change any score.

  6. Build the per-cell table. All paired values in one long data frame.

  7. Summarize per group. Effect, the three distribution measures, optional sign-flip null calibration, leading genes, and the two priority rankings. Benjamini–Hochberg FDR is applied separately within each group × method.

  8. Record state under seurat_obj@misc[[misc_name]], optionally writing RDS and CSV to out_dir.

What comes back

With return_details = TRUE you get a list:

names(alert_v2)
# "seurat"  "per_cell"  "metrics"  "gene_sets"  "params"  "info_file"  "metrics_file"

With return_details = FALSE (the default) you get the Seurat object back, and the same content lives in @misc:

names(alert_v2$seurat@misc$AlertSystem)
# "schema_version"  "per_cell"  "metrics"  "gene_sets"  "params"

per_cell — the paired, cell-level table 

head(alert_v2$per_cell)
Column Meaning
cell cell barcode
group value of group.by, or "all_cells"
sample value of sample.by, or NA
pathway gene set name
score_method "expression" or "ucell"
change_measure how the response was computed (e.g. difference, log2_ratio)
pre_score baseline pathway score for this cell
post_score perturbed pathway score for this cell
delta post_score - pre_score (or the log2 ratio)

This table is the raw material for any custom analysis — the response distribution for a single pathway, per-cell scatter of two pathways, or mapping delta back onto the UMAP coordinates we added earlier.

metrics — the group-level summary

One row per group × pathway × score_method. This is what AlertHeatmap() reads, and what you should export for the supplement.

alert_v2$metrics %>%
  filter(score_method == "expression") %>%
  arrange(desc(widespread_priority)) %>%
  select(pathway, effect, response_rate, directional_consistency,
         robust_fraction, null_z, empirical_p, fdr) %>%
  head(10)

params — provenance

Every argument you passed, plus compact_version, seurat_version, ucell_version and a timestamp. Record this in your methods section; it is the difference between a reproducible figure and a figure you will have to regenerate from memory.

alert_v2$params$summary_fun
alert_v2$params$expression_response_threshold
alert_v2$params$compact_version
alert_v2$params$timestamp

The metrics table, column by column

This is the heart of the Alert System, so it is worth going through every column. They fall into six families.

1. Identity and size

Column Definition
group the group.by level (or "all_cells")
pathway gene set name
score_method "expression" or "ucell"
change_measure the response transformation used
n_cells cells contributing to this row
n_samples distinct sample.by values, when supplied

2. The effect and its distribution

Column Definition
effect the headline group-level response, computed with summary_fun
mean_delta arithmetic mean of per-cell delta
median_delta median of per-cell delta
trimmed_mean_delta mean after removing trim from each tail
q10_delta, q90_delta 10th and 90th percentiles of per-cell delta

effect is one of mean_delta / median_delta / trimmed_mean_delta depending on summary_fun; the other three are always reported so you can see how much the choice matters. The default, "trimmed_mean", is the right default: single-cell pathway deltas have heavy tails, and a plain mean can be dragged by a handful of cells. If mean_delta and trimmed_mean_delta disagree sharply for a pathway, that pathway’s response is concentrated in a small number of cells — which is exactly what focal_priority below is designed to find.

3. The three distribution measures

These are the measures described in the methods, and they are the reason the Alert System says more than a fold-change.

Column Definition
response_threshold the threshold in force for this channel
response_rate fraction of all cells with |delta| ≥ threshold
directional_consistency among responding cells, fraction whose sign matches sign(effect)
robust_fraction fraction of all cells that both respond and match sign(effect)
opposite_fraction fraction of all cells that respond with the opposite sign
tie_fraction fraction of responding cells with no resolvable direction
concordance_all direction agreement computed over all cells, not only responders

directional_consistency is NA when effect is exactly zero or no cell responds; robust_fraction and opposite_fraction are 0 under the same conditions.

Read them as a triple:

  • High response_rate, high directional_consistency → a coherent, population-wide program shift. This is the signature you want to report.
  • Low response_rate, high directional_consistency → a focal response: a minority of cells move, but they all move the same way. Easy to miss in a group mean, and often the most interesting biology in a vulnerability screen.
  • High response_rate, low directional_consistency → cells are responding but disagreeing. Usually heterogeneity you have not modeled yet (a cell state or lineage splitting the response); try group.by.
  • High opposite_fraction → an explicit warning that the group-level sign is averaging over two populations moving in opposite directions. Do not report the group effect for such a pathway without splitting the group.

4. Calibration

Column Definition
calibration_effect the statistic the null was built around
null_center center of the sign-flip null distribution
null_scale spread of the sign-flip null distribution
null_z standardized effect, (calibration_effect − null_center) / null_scale
empirical_p two-sided empirical p-value from n_permutations sign flips
fdr Benjamini–Hochberg FDR, computed within each group × score_method

The null is a two-sided sign-flip permutation: the signs of the paired responses are randomly flipped, which is the correct null for a paired design (“the perturbation moved this pathway in no particular direction”). By default the flips are applied at the sample level — see Statistical calibration for why that matters.

5. Gene coverage and leading genes

Column Definition
genes_in_set size of the original gene set
genes_used genes retained after intersecting with both assays
gene_coverage genes_used / genes_in_set
n_direct_overlap pathway genes changed directly by the perturbation
n_propagated_overlap pathway genes changed only through propagation
gene_direction_fraction fraction of pathway genes moving with the effect
leading_genes top leading_n genes by mean gene-level change

n_direct_overlap is the circularity check. If a pathway’s response is driven mostly by genes you perturbed directly — the module’s own hub genes — then the Alert System is reporting your input back to you. A pathway with a high n_propagated_overlap and a low n_direct_overlap is a genuinely downstream consequence of the module change, and that is the claim worth making.

# pathways whose response is mostly propagated, not directly imposed
alert_v2$metrics %>%
  filter(score_method == "expression", fdr <= 0.05) %>%
  mutate(propagated_share = n_propagated_overlap /
           pmax(n_direct_overlap + n_propagated_overlap, 1)) %>%
  filter(propagated_share > 0.8) %>%
  arrange(desc(widespread_priority)) %>%
  select(pathway, effect, propagated_share, n_direct_overlap,
         n_propagated_overlap, leading_genes)

6. The two priority scores

These exist because no single number ranks pathways well. They combine strength, breadth and coherence in two different ways.

widespread_priority — find programs that moved across the population.

standardized_strength = |null_z|                       if calibration available
                      = |effect| / threshold           if threshold > 0
                      = |effect|                       otherwise

consistency_signal    = max(0, 2 * directional_consistency - 1)
                      = 0                              if not finite

widespread_priority   = standardized_strength * sqrt(response_rate) * consistency_signal

The 2c − 1 term is the key design choice: a pathway at 50% directional consistency is a coin flip and scores zero, no matter how large its effect. The sqrt(response_rate) term rewards breadth with diminishing returns, so a pathway responding in 80% of cells is not ranked four times above one responding in 20%.

focal_priority — find programs that moved hard in a minority of cells.

focal_tail      = max(0, 90th percentile of (sign(effect) * delta))
                = 0                                     if effect == 0

focal_priority  = (focal_tail / threshold) * sqrt(robust_fraction)   if threshold > 0
                = focal_tail * sqrt(robust_fraction)                 otherwise

Here the magnitude comes from the tail of the direction-adjusted response rather than its center, so a pathway that barely moves on average but moves dramatically in the top decile of cells rises to the top. This is the ranking to use when you are hunting for vulnerable subpopulations — the cells that would have been lost to selection in a real experiment, which is precisely the population we suspect is missing from the Ufd1l data.

# compare the two rankings side by side
bind_rows(
  alert_v2$metrics %>% filter(score_method == "expression") %>%
    arrange(desc(widespread_priority)) %>% head(10) %>%
    mutate(ranking = "widespread"),
  alert_v2$metrics %>% filter(score_method == "expression") %>%
    arrange(desc(focal_priority)) %>% head(10) %>%
    mutate(ranking = "focal")
) %>%
  select(ranking, pathway, effect, response_rate, robust_fraction,
         widespread_priority, focal_priority)

Pathways appearing in the focal list but not the widespread list are the candidates for the hidden-vulnerability narrative: real, coherent, and invisible to a group mean.

Choosing a response threshold

expression_response_threshold (default 0.01) and ucell_response_threshold (default 0.005 for differences, 0.1 for log2 ratios) define what counts as “a cell responded”. Everything in family 3 above, and both priority scores, depends on it — so it should be a deliberate choice, not an inherited default.

A practical way to set it is to look at the response distribution itself:

alert_v2$per_cell %>%
  filter(score_method == "expression") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = abs(delta))) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.01, linetype = "dashed", color = "#CC4C4C") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "|pathway response| (log10)", y = "density")

You are looking for a value that sits above the bulk of the near-zero mass but below the shoulder of real responses. A useful sanity check is to rescore with a modestly stricter threshold:

alert_strict <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj, gene_sets, perturbation_name = "M6_up",
  score_methods = "expression",
  expression_response_threshold = 0.03,
  null_unit = "auto", n_permutations = 2000,
  misc_name = "AlertSystem_strict",
  return_details = TRUE
)

If a pathway’s rank collapses under a 3× stricter threshold, its response_rate was being carried by cells sitting just above the cutoff.

A note on scale. The threshold is on the same scale as delta, which for the expression channel is a mean log-normalized difference averaged over pathway genes. That number is small by construction — averaging over 100+ genes shrinks it — so 0.01 is a meaningful amount of movement, not a rounding error. UCell scores are bounded rank statistics on a different scale entirely, which is why they get their own threshold.

Statistical calibration

This section matters more than any other for how you write up the result.

Cells are not replicates

The Alert System happily scores thousands of cells, and the per-cell distribution measures (response_rate, directional_consistency, robust_fraction) are descriptive statistics of that distribution — they are the point of the method and they are valid as described.

But p-values are a different matter. Cells from one animal are not independent replicates of the biological condition. The source code is explicit about this: cell-level null calibration is labeled descriptive, and inferential calibration is intended to run at the sample level.

null_unit = "auto"      # samples when sample.by is supplied; otherwise no calibration
null_unit = "sample"    # force sample-level sign flips (inferential)
null_unit = "cell"      # force cell-level sign flips (DESCRIPTIVE ONLY)
null_unit = "none"      # skip calibration entirely

With null_unit = "auto" and no sample.by, calibration is disabled — this is a deliberate guardrail, not a bug. null_z, empirical_p and fdr will be NA, and widespread_priority will fall back to |effect| / threshold for its strength term.

Recommendation: if your design has replicates, pass them. We checked table(seurat_obj$lane) earlier for exactly this reason:

alert_calibrated <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj        = seurat_obj,
  gene_sets         = gene_sets,
  perturbation_name = "M6_up",
  baseline_assay    = "RNA",

  group.by  = "cell_types_broad",   # score within each neuronal class
  sample.by = "lane",               # or "donor_id", "animal", "batch"

  score_methods = "expression",
  summary_fun   = "trimmed_mean",
  trim          = 0.1,

  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  null_unit      = "sample",
  n_permutations = 2000,
  return_details = TRUE
)

If you genuinely have one sample — a pooled screen with no replication — run with null_unit = "none", rank by widespread_priority and focal_priority, and describe the result as a prioritization rather than a test. That is an honest and perfectly publishable framing for pilot data, and it fits the way this analysis is used: to flag signatures worth following up and to refine experimental design before committing resources to a larger experiment.

group.by

Supplying group.by scores each level separately, with its own effect, its own null, and its own FDR correction. Use it whenever the response plausibly differs between cell types — which, for a module perturbation across deep-layer, superficial-layer and interneuron populations, is likely. Watch sample_consistency: it reports the fraction of per-sample effects whose sign matches the group effect, and a value near 0.5 means your group-level effect is not reproducible across samples regardless of what the p-value says.

Visualizing with AlertHeatmap 

perturbation_name <- 'M6_up'

p_widespread <- AlertHeatmap(
  alert_v2$seurat,
  score_method     = "expression",
  top_n            = 20,
  side             = "both",
  select_by        = "widespread_priority",
  fill_by          = "effect",
  show_annotations = TRUE,
  show_fdr         = TRUE
)

pdf(paste0(AS_dir, 'AlertHeatmap_', perturbation_name, '.pdf'), width = 5, height = 12)
p_widespread
dev.off()

AlertHeatmap() reads seurat_obj@misc[[misc_name]]$metrics directly — you pass the Seurat object, not the metrics table.

Reading the plot

  • Rows are pathways, selected by select_by and ordered by reorder_by.
  • Columns are the levels of group.by (a single all_cells column if you did not group).
  • Tile fill is effect (native response units) or null_z (standardized).
  • In-tile annotations, when show_annotations = TRUE, are r = response_rate and c = directional_consistency. These are what make the heatmap more informative than a standard pathway heatmap: a deeply colored tile with r = 0.08 is a focal response, not a population-wide one.
  • Asterisks, when show_fdr = TRUE, mark fdr <= fdr_cutoff (default 0.05). With no sample.by, there will be no asterisks — see Statistical calibration.

Selection, scaling and the focal view

top_n is applied separately to each requested side, so side = "both" with top_n = 20 gives up to 40 rows — 20 up, 20 down.

Two arguments are worth knowing about. scale_mode = "unit" divides by a robust magnitude (the unit_q quantile of absolute displayed values, default 0.9) and clips to [-1, 1]; use it when a single dominant pathway is flattening the color scale. We use it for the combined perturbation below. For a figure panel where several perturbations must share one scale, fix fill_limits explicitly instead:

AlertHeatmap(alert_v2$seurat, fill_limits = c(-0.05, 0.05), ...)

Swapping select_by switches between the two narratives:

# the same data ranked for minority-but-strong responses
AlertHeatmap(
  alert_v2$seurat,
  score_method     = "expression",
  top_n            = 15,
  side             = "both",
  select_by        = "focal_priority",
  fill_by          = "effect",
  show_annotations = TRUE,
  show_fdr         = TRUE
)

Pathways that appear under focal_priority but not widespread_priority are your hidden-vulnerability candidates.

Combining perturbations

Real module changes rarely happen one at a time. The surviving Ufd1l nuclei show a combined module upregulation and a downregulation of CBh-M1 relative to control, so scoring each perturbation separately answers a different question than scoring the joint state. CombinePerturbAssays() builds that joint assay.

# clear any previous Alert System state so results are not silently mixed
seurat_obj@misc$AlertSystem <- NULL
"AlertSystem" %in% names(seurat_obj@misc)
# [1] FALSE

seurat_obj <- CombinePerturbAssays(
  seurat_obj,
  perturb_assays = c("M6_up", "M1_down"),
  baseline_assay = "RNA",
  new_assay      = "M6up_M1down"
)

What combining actually does

Perturbation assays are mixed-layer objects: direct targets are changed in the counts layer, while secondary genes are changed by network propagation in the log-normalized data layer. Naively adding two such assays would double-count. CombinePerturbAssays() instead:

  1. adds the count-space deltas from each assay to the baseline counts,
  2. log-normalizes the result using the baseline library sizes (so the normalization is not itself perturbed), and
  3. adds each assay’s data-space delta only for genes not directly changed in that assay.

Step 3 is what keeps secondary effects intact when a gene is a direct target in one perturbation and a propagated gene in the other. Provenance metadata is written to the new assay’s misc slot.

Useful arguments:

Argument Default Why you’d change it
new_assay "<assays>_combined" name it for the figure
scale.factor 1e4 match a non-standard normalization
direct_tolerance 0 a gene is “direct” if any cell’s count change exceeds this
check_provenance TRUE verify each input was built from baseline_assay
require_provenance FALSE set TRUE to hard-fail on unstamped assays
floor_counts / floor_data TRUE zero out negatives; FALSE errors instead
overwrite FALSE replace an existing assay of the same name

If check_provenance = TRUE and strict_provenance_check = TRUE (both defaults), a stamp that conflicts with baseline_assay or lacks the counts layer stops the function. Set strict_provenance_check = FALSE to downgrade that to a warning — but understand why the stamp disagrees before you do.

Score the combined assay 

alert_v2_combined <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj        = seurat_obj,
  gene_sets         = gene_sets,
  perturbation_name = "M6up_M1down",
  baseline_assay    = "RNA",

  # group.by = "cell_types_broad",
  # sample.by = "lane",

  score_methods = "expression",
  summary_fun   = "trimmed_mean",
  trim          = 0.1,

  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  ucell_response_threshold      = 0.005,

  null_unit      = "auto",
  n_permutations = 2000,

  return_details = TRUE
)

p_widespread2 <- AlertHeatmap(
  alert_v2_combined$seurat,
  score_method     = "expression",
  top_n            = 15,
  scale_mode       = "unit",
  unit_q           = 0.9,
  side             = "both",
  select_by        = "widespread_priority",
  fill_by          = "effect",
  show_annotations = TRUE,
  show_fdr         = TRUE
)

pdf(paste0(AS_dir, 'AlertHeatmap_M6up_M1down_v2_top15.pdf'), width = 5, height = 8)
p_widespread2
dev.off()

This is the result the whole workflow was building toward. The joint module change predicts increased expression of genes associated with the unfolded protein response, hypoxia, inflammatory and glycolytic programs, accompanied by decreased expression of the oxidative phosphorylation program.

That is a coordinated stress signature, and it connects back to the original observation in two ways. The predicted unfolded protein response is consistent with the proteostasis-related enrichment reported for Ufd1l in the original study — which is the reason it was set aside. The accompanying hypoxia- and metabolism-associated changes suggest something broader: a disruption of cellular homeostasis of the kind that would plausibly make a neuron vulnerable, and plausibly cause the most affected nuclei to be lost before sequencing.

Is the combination more than the sum of its parts?

Scoring all three assays lets you ask whether the joint perturbation produces a response the single perturbations do not:

score_one <- function(assay) {
  AlertSystemScore(
    seurat_obj, gene_sets, perturbation_name = assay,
    baseline_assay = "RNA", score_methods = "expression",
    expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
    null_unit = "none", misc_name = paste0("AS_", assay),
    return_details = TRUE, verbose = FALSE
  )$metrics %>%
    filter(score_method == "expression") %>%
    select(pathway, effect, response_rate) %>%
    rename_with(~paste0(.x, "_", assay), -pathway)
}

comparison <- reduce(
  map(c("M6_up", "M1_down", "M6up_M1down"), score_one),
  full_join, by = "pathway"
) %>%
  mutate(interaction = effect_M6up_M1down - (effect_M6_up + effect_M1_down)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(interaction)))

head(comparison, 15)

A large interaction term flags pathways where the two module changes are not additive — the joint state does something neither module does alone. Treat this as hypothesis generation rather than a formal interaction test.

Important. Always clear or rename the Alert System state between runs. misc_name defaults to "AlertSystem" for every call, so a second AlertSystemScore() on the same object will overwrite the first, and an AlertHeatmap() call will silently plot whichever ran last. Either set seurat_obj@misc$AlertSystem <- NULL between runs, or give each run its own misc_name.

Note also that perturbation_name must name an existing assay. If you named the combined assay "M6up_M1down", that exact string is what AlertSystemScore() needs — a suffixed variant will not resolve.

The UCell channel

The expression channel averages log-normalized differences, which makes it sensitive to the absolute magnitude of expression change and to highly expressed pathway genes. UCell instead computes a rank-based signature score per cell, which is robust to depth and to a few dominant genes. Running both is a strong robustness check: a pathway that tops both rankings is not an artifact of the scoring scale.

alert_v2_combined2 <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj        = seurat_obj,
  gene_sets         = gene_sets,
  perturbation_name = "M6up_M1down",
  baseline_assay    = "RNA",

  # group.by = "cell_types_broad",
  # sample.by = "lane",

  score_methods = "ucell",
  ucell_change  = "log2_ratio",
  trim          = 0.1,

  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  ucell_response_threshold      = 0.005,

  null_unit      = "auto",
  n_permutations = 2000,

  return_details = TRUE
)

p_widespread4 <- AlertHeatmap(
  alert_v2_combined2$seurat,
  score_method     = "ucell",
  top_n            = 50,
  scale_mode       = "unit",
  unit_q           = 0.9,
  side             = "both",
  select_by        = "widespread_priority",
  fill_by          = "effect",
  show_annotations = TRUE,
  show_fdr         = TRUE
)

difference vs. log2_ratio

ucell_change Response Default threshold When to use
"difference" post - pre 0.005 the default; symmetric, interpretable in UCell units
"log2_ratio" log2((post + pc) / (pre + pc)) 0.1 when baseline scores vary widely across cells and you want relative change

The pseudocount ucell_pseudocount (default 1e-4) stabilizes the ratio for cells with near-zero baseline scores, and is used only for "log2_ratio".

Set the threshold to match the channel. The call above passes ucell_change = "log2_ratio" together with ucell_response_threshold = 0.005, which is a difference-scale value. On the log2-ratio scale that threshold is very permissive, so nearly every cell will count as responding and response_rate becomes uninformative. Leaving ucell_response_threshold = NULL lets the function pick the right default (0.1) for the transformation you chose — the safest option:

  ucell_change             = "log2_ratio",
  ucell_response_threshold = NULL,   # -> 0.1, the log2-ratio default

Scoring both channels in one call keeps them in a single metrics table:

alert_both <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj, gene_sets, perturbation_name = "M6up_M1down",
  score_methods = c("expression", "ucell"),
  ucell_change = "difference",
  ucell_response_threshold = NULL,
  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  null_unit = "auto", n_permutations = 2000,
  return_details = TRUE
)

# pathways prioritized by both channels
alert_both$metrics %>%
  select(pathway, score_method, widespread_priority) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = score_method, values_from = widespread_priority) %>%
  arrange(desc(pmin(expression, ucell))) %>%
  head(15)

FDR is computed within each group and each score method, so the two channels are corrected independently — as they should be, since they are two views of the same data rather than two additional tests.

Saving and reloading

Scoring with 2000 permutations over a full hallmark collection is not free. Persist the state so figures can be regenerated without rescoring.

Automatic export 

alert_v2 <- AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj, gene_sets, perturbation_name = "M6_up",
  score_methods     = "expression",
  out_dir           = AS_dir,
  output_prefix     = "Ufd1l_M6up",     # defaults to a sanitized perturbation name
  overwrite_outputs = FALSE,
  return_details    = TRUE
)

alert_v2$info_file      # RDS of the complete state
alert_v2$metrics_file   # CSV of the metrics table

overwrite_outputs = FALSE refuses to clobber existing files — keep it that way until you are sure you want to replace a figure’s source data.

Manual save and load 

SaveAlertSystem(
  seurat_obj,
  file      = paste0(AS_dir, "AlertSystem_M6_up.rds"),
  misc_name = "AlertSystem",
  overwrite = FALSE
)

# later, or in a fresh session
seurat_obj <- LoadAlertSystem(
  seurat_obj,
  file              = paste0(AS_dir, "AlertSystem_M6_up.rds"),
  misc_name         = "AlertSystem",
  overwrite         = TRUE,
  require_gene_sets = FALSE,
  verbose           = TRUE
)

# AlertHeatmap(seurat_obj, score_method = "expression", top_n = 20)

SaveAlertSystem() refuses to overwrite unless overwrite = TRUE, creates the parent directory if needed, and returns the normalized path invisibly. LoadAlertSystem() validates the state (per_cell, metrics, params, and gene_sets when require_gene_sets = TRUE) before attaching it. It does not add score columns to meta.data — the state lives in @misc only.

Full parameter reference

Show the full parameter reference — every argument and default for AlertSystemScore(), AlertHeatmap(), CombinePerturbAssays(), and the pathway/state helpers

AlertSystemScore() 

AlertSystemScore(
  seurat_obj,
  gene_sets,
  perturbation_name,
  baseline_assay = "RNA",
  group.by = NULL,
  sample.by = NULL,
  layer = "data",
  min_genes = 5L,
  score_methods = c("expression", "ucell"),
  ucell_change = c("difference", "log2_ratio"),
  ucell_pseudocount = 1e-4,
  summary_fun = c("trimmed_mean", "median", "mean"),
  trim = 0.1,
  expression_response_threshold = 0.01,
  ucell_response_threshold = NULL,
  null_unit = c("auto", "sample", "cell", "none"),
  n_permutations = 1000L,
  seed = 1L,
  leading_n = 5L,
  gene_change_tolerance = 1e-8,
  misc_name = "AlertSystem",
  out_dir = NULL,
  output_prefix = NULL,
  overwrite_outputs = FALSE,
  return_details = FALSE,
  verbose = TRUE
)
Argument Default Notes
seurat_obj — must contain baseline and perturbation assays
gene_sets — named list of gene vectors
perturbation_name — name of the perturbed assay
baseline_assay "RNA" the pre state
group.by NULL metadata column; NULL → one "all_cells" group
sample.by NULL biological replicate column; strongly recommended
layer "data" log-normalized layer used by expression scoring
min_genes 5L pathways below this (after intersection) are dropped
score_methods c("expression","ucell") pass one or both
ucell_change "difference" or "log2_ratio"
ucell_pseudocount 1e-4 used only for "log2_ratio"
summary_fun "trimmed_mean" also "median", "mean"
trim 0.1 tail fraction removed per side
expression_response_threshold 0.01 defines “responded” for the expression channel
ucell_response_threshold NULL NULL → 0.005 (difference) or 0.1 (log2 ratio)
null_unit "auto" "auto" uses samples if sample.by given, else disables
n_permutations 1000L 2000+ for stable empirical p-values
seed 1L seeds the null and temporary UCell column names
leading_n 5L leading genes recorded per pathway × group
gene_change_tolerance 1e-8 direct vs. propagated classification tolerance
misc_name "AlertSystem" change it per run to avoid overwriting
out_dir NULL when set, writes RDS + CSV
output_prefix NULL defaults to a sanitized perturbation name
overwrite_outputs FALSE guard against clobbering figure source data
return_details FALSE TRUE returns the full list
verbose TRUE progress messages

AlertHeatmap() 

AlertHeatmap(
  seurat_obj,
  misc_name = "AlertSystem",
  score_method = c("expression", "ucell"),
  top_n = 5L,
  side = c("both", "positive", "negative"),
  select_by = c("widespread_priority", "focal_priority", "abs_effect",
                "null_z", "robust_fraction", "response_rate"),
  fill_by = c("effect", "null_z"),
  reorder_by = c("effect", "select"),
  scale_mode = c("none", "unit"),
  unit_q = 0.9,
  show_annotations = TRUE,
  show_fdr = TRUE,
  fdr_cutoff = 0.05,
  fill_limits = NULL
)

CombinePerturbAssays() 

CombinePerturbAssays(
  seurat_obj,
  perturb_assays,
  baseline_assay = "RNA",
  new_assay = paste0(paste(perturb_assays, collapse = "_"), "_combined"),
  scale.factor = 1e4,
  direct_tolerance = 0,
  check_provenance = TRUE,
  require_provenance = FALSE,
  strict_provenance_check = TRUE,
  floor_counts = TRUE,
  floor_data = TRUE,
  allow_dense = FALSE,
  overwrite = FALSE,
  verbose = TRUE
)

LoadAlertSystemPathways() / SaveAlertSystem() / LoadAlertSystem() 

LoadAlertSystemPathways(
  path = NULL,
  genetype = c("mouse", "human"),
  database = "MSigDBhallmark",
  package = "compact",
  allow_download = TRUE,
  github_base = <package default>,
  verbose = TRUE
)

SaveAlertSystem(seurat_obj, file, misc_name = "AlertSystem", overwrite = FALSE)

LoadAlertSystem(seurat_obj, file, misc_name = "AlertSystem",
                overwrite = TRUE, require_gene_sets = FALSE, verbose = TRUE)

Resolution order for LoadAlertSystemPathways() is path → the package’s inst/extdata → GitHub download (allow_download = TRUE), looking for <database>_gene_sets_<genetype>.rds.

Troubleshooting

Show the troubleshooting table — common symptoms, their causes, and what to change
Symptom Likely cause Fix
null_z, empirical_p, fdr all NA null_unit = "auto" with no sample.by supply sample.by, or set null_unit = "sample" / "none" deliberately
No asterisks on the heatmap same as above see above
Heatmap shows the wrong perturbation misc_name collision between runs set a distinct misc_name per run, or NULL the old state
perturbation_name not found name does not match an existing assay check Assays(seurat_obj)
Many pathways dropped min_genes vs. sparse detection check gene_coverage; confirm the gene sets’ species matches the object
UCell results look degenerate threshold on the wrong scale leave ucell_response_threshold = NULL
response_rate near 1.0 for everything threshold too low inspect the abs(delta) density and raise it
directional_consistency near 0.5 unmodeled heterogeneity add group.by; check opposite_fraction
Top pathways are all module hub genes circularity filter on n_propagated_overlap vs. n_direct_overlap
CombinePerturbAssays errors on provenance assays built from a different baseline confirm the baseline, or set strict_provenance_check = FALSE knowingly

Reporting checklist

When writing up an Alert System result, state:

  1. the pathway database and version (MSigDBhallmark, species, MSigDB release);
  2. min_genes and the observed gene_coverage range;
  3. the scoring channel(s) and, for UCell, the ucell_change transformation;
  4. summary_fun and trim;
  5. the response threshold for each channel;
  6. null_unit, sample.by, and n_permutations — or an explicit statement that the analysis is a prioritization rather than a test;
  7. whether ranking used widespread_priority or focal_priority;
  8. the direct/propagated split for the pathways you highlight;
  9. the separate provenance of upstream tools — Mixscale is its own package and should be cited independently of compact.
